cards.title: Stack (LIFO)
cards.teaser: A stack is a last-in, first-out container — the last element you pushed is the first one you get back, which makes it the natural data structure for anything that needs to reverse order or remember "where I came from."

runs.text: A stack is an abstract data type with one defining property:
. You can only interact with the top element. You push items onto the top and pop them off the top. You cannot access anything in the middle without removing everything above it first.
The operations and their complexity on a properly implemented stack:

items.text: — remove and return the top — O(1)
— read the top without removing it — O(1)
— check whether the stack has no elements — O(1)

runs.text: Stacks appear whenever a process needs to reverse a sequence, defer work, or track the path back to a starting point. Classic use cases include:

items.text: The call stack — each function call is pushed; each return pops
Undo/redo — each action is pushed onto the undo stack
Parentheses matching — push open brackets, pop on close
DFS traversal — push neighbors to explore, pop to advance

runs.text: "Stack" refers to the abstract behavior (LIFO), not any specific implementation. Python's list, a linked list, or a fixed-size array can all implement a stack correctly — the difference is in the constant factors, not the complexity class.

A stack is a Pringles can: you always add to the top and take from the top. The chip you put in last is the first one you reach for. You cannot grab the chip at the bottom without eating everything above it first.

cards.title: Stack Operations: push, pop, peek, isEmpty
cards.teaser: Every stack exposes exactly four operations — push, pop, peek, and isEmpty — and every one of them is O(1). The entire power of the data structure comes from enforcing that you only ever touch the top.

runs.text: Stack operations are intentionally limited. The constraint is the point — by refusing to allow arbitrary access, the stack makes certain algorithms simple and correct by construction.

items.text: — Places an item on top of the stack. If you imagine a stack of trays in a cafeteria, this is sliding a new tray onto the top of the spring-loaded dispenser.
— Removes and returns the top item. If the stack is empty, this raises an error (or returns None, depending on implementation). The caller is responsible for checking first.
— Returns the top item without removing it. Also called
in some libraries. Useful when you need to inspect before deciding whether to pop.
— Returns True if the stack contains no items. Always check this before pop or peek to avoid errors.

explanation.code:
stack = []

# push
stack.append("a")
stack.append("b")
stack.append("c")  # stack is now ["a", "b", "c"]

# peek
top = stack[-1]    # "c" — no removal

# isEmpty
if stack:          # truthy check is idiomatic isEmpty()
    top = stack.pop()  # "c" — removed

print(stack)       # ["a", "b"]

runs.text: (with no argument) pops from the end — both are O(1) amortized. Using
gives you peek. There is no separate Stack class in the standard library because list already does the job perfectly.

Think of a stack of books on a desk. Push means set a new book on top. Pop means take the top book away. Peek means read the title of the top book without picking it up. isEmpty means check whether there are any books left. You never touch anything except the top book.

cards.title: Stack Implementation with Python list
cards.teaser: Python's list is the idiomatic stack in Python — append() is push, pop() is pop, and both are O(1) amortized because list grows from the right end, making the top of the stack the cheapest place to insert and remove.

runs.text: Python's built-in list supports all four stack operations natively and efficiently. Because a list stores elements contiguously in memory and tracks only the end pointer, appending and popping from the right end are both O(1) amortized — no shifting, no reallocation on every operation.
The wrapper class is optional. In production Python, most developers use a bare list and call
directly. The class form is useful when you want to:

items.text: Prevent callers from using list operations (indexing, insert) that violate LIFO discipline
Add bounded capacity (raise on overflow) for resource-limited contexts
Make the data structure's intent self-documenting in the type signature

runs.text: as pop — those are O(n) because they shift every element. Keep the top of the stack at the right end of the list.

Using a Python list as a stack is like using a whiteboard as a to-do list that you always add to and erase from the bottom — the most recently written item is always at the bottom of the board (the end of the list), and that is the only item you ever touch.

cards.title: The Call Stack
cards.teaser: Every time you call a function, the runtime pushes a stack frame onto the call stack — local variables, the return address, and parameters all live in that frame. When the function returns, the frame is popped, and execution resumes exactly where it left off.

runs.text: The call stack is the concrete stack that every running program uses to track function invocations. It is not a library data structure — it is a region of memory managed by the operating system and the language runtime.
(also called an activation record) that contains:

items.text: The arguments passed to the function
The return address — where execution resumes after the function finishes
A reference to the calling frame (the frame below)

runs.text: Each return pops a frame. When
returns 1, its frame is popped and the result is handed back to
, which resumes, computes 1 × 1, pops its frame, and so on up the stack.

Stack overflow is not a website — it is a real error: you exceeded the call stack's size limit. Python's default recursion limit is 1000 frames. Deep recursion on large inputs hits this limit. The fix is either increasing the limit with
(use sparingly) or converting to an iterative solution with an explicit stack.

The call stack is like a pile of sticky notes on your desk. When you call a function, you write down what you were doing and put a new sticky note on top. When the function returns, you throw away the top note and look at the one underneath to remember what you were doing before.

cards.title: Queue (FIFO)
cards.teaser: A queue is a first-in, first-out container — the first element you enqueue is the first one you dequeue. It models any real-world waiting line: print jobs, network packets, BFS traversal nodes, background task workers.

runs.text: A queue is an abstract data type with one defining property:
. New items join at the back (rear); items leave from the front. The element that has been waiting longest is always the next to be served.
The operations and their complexity on a properly implemented queue:

items.text: — remove and return from the front — O(1)
— inspect the front element without removing it — O(1)
— check whether the queue has no elements — O(1)
BFS traversal — nodes are enqueued by level and dequeued in order
Task queues (Celery, RabbitMQ, SQS) — jobs enter at the back, workers consume from the front
Rate limiting — request timestamps are queued to count how many arrived in the last N seconds
Printer spooler — jobs print in the order they were submitted

runs.text: A queue is a checkout line at a grocery store. The first shopper in line is the first to be served. New shoppers join at the back. Nobody cuts to the front. FIFO is enforced by the structure, not by politeness.

cards.title: Queue Operations: enqueue, dequeue, front
cards.teaser: A queue's three core operations — enqueue, dequeue, and front — are all O(1) on a correct implementation. Getting them right means knowing which end is which, and why it matters for performance.

runs.text: A queue has two ends that serve different roles. This asymmetry is fundamental — it is what produces FIFO behavior.

items.text: in some APIs. Must be O(1) — any implementation that shifts elements on enqueue is wrong.
— removes and returns the item from the

— reads the front item without removing it. Equivalent to

explanation.code:
from collections import deque

q = deque()

# enqueue — add to the right (rear)
q.append("first")
q.append("second")
q.append("third")

# front — inspect without removing
print(q[0])        # "first"

# dequeue — remove from the left (front)
print(q.popleft()) # "first" — FIFO
print(q.popleft()) # "second"
print(len(q))      # 1

runs.text: The naming inconsistency in Python's stdlib is real:
is dequeue. The method names describe the
data structure, not the queue abstraction. This is idiomatic Python — just remember: append to the right, popleft from the left.

A queue is a one-way tube: items enter on the right and exit on the left. Enqueue shoves an item in the right end, dequeue pulls an item out the left end, and front lets you look through the left opening without pulling anything out.

cards.title: collections.deque for O(1) Queue Operations
cards.teaser: Python's collections.deque is the correct queue implementation — it delivers O(1) append to the right and O(1) popleft from the left, because it is a doubly-linked list of fixed-size blocks, not a contiguous array.

runs.text: (pronounced "deck," short for double-ended queue) is the right tool for queue workloads in Python. Its internal structure is a doubly-linked list of fixed-size blocks (each holding ~64 elements on CPython). This gives it O(1) operations at both ends.

explanation.code:
from collections import deque

# BFS skeleton using deque as a queue
def bfs(graph, start):
    visited = set()
    queue = deque([start])
    visited.add(start)

    while queue:
        node = queue.popleft()          # O(1) dequeue
        print(node)
        for neighbor in graph[node]:
            if neighbor not in visited:
                visited.add(neighbor)
                queue.append(neighbor)  # O(1) enqueue

# Optional: bound the queue with maxlen
bounded = deque(maxlen=100)  # oldest items auto-evicted on overflow

items.text: O(n) for random indexing — not a list replacement when you need
parameter makes it a bounded circular buffer — old items auto-evict

runs.text: A deque is like a train with doors at both ends — passengers can board and exit from either the front or the back in O(1) time. When you use it as a queue, you only board at the back and exit at the front, giving you pure FIFO. The train design makes both doors equally fast.

cards.title: Why Python list as Queue is O(n)
cards.teaser: Using a Python list as a queue — with append() to enqueue and pop(0) to dequeue — looks correct but is O(n) per dequeue, because removing from index 0 forces Python to shift every remaining element one position to the left.

runs.text: works correctly — it always returns the first element. The problem is performance. A Python list is a contiguous array in memory. When you remove the element at index 0, CPython must copy every remaining element one slot to the left so that index 0 still points to valid memory. That is O(n) for a list of n elements.

explanation.code:
import time

# Correct but slow: O(n) per dequeue
queue_list = list(range(100_000))
start = time.perf_counter()
while queue_list:
    queue_list.pop(0)   # O(n) — shifts all remaining elements
print(f"list: {time.perf_counter() - start:.3f}s")

# Correct and fast: O(1) per dequeue
from collections import deque
queue_deque = deque(range(100_000))
start = time.perf_counter()
while queue_deque:
    queue_deque.popleft()  # O(1) — pointer update only
print(f"deque: {time.perf_counter() - start:.3f}s")

# Typical result: list is 100-1000x slower at this size

items.text: : draining 100 000 elements is O(n²) total — roughly 5 billion element copies
: draining 100 000 elements is O(n) total — 100 000 pointer updates

Using pop(0) on a list is like removing the first person from a physical line by having everyone else physically shuffle one step forward after each departure. It works, but if a thousand people are in line, each departure causes a thousand shuffle steps. A deque is like a rope with a sliding front marker — the marker moves, nobody shuffles.

cards.title: Priority Queue
cards.teaser: A priority queue is a queue where dequeue always returns the highest-priority element — not the oldest one. Python's heapq module implements a min-heap that makes the smallest item the highest priority, giving O(log n) insert and O(log n) extract.

runs.text: A priority queue breaks the FIFO guarantee: instead of serving items in arrival order, it always serves the item with the highest priority. The underlying data structure is almost always a
— a complete binary tree that maintains the heap property (each parent is smaller than its children for a min-heap).

explanation.code:
import heapq

# heapq is a min-heap: smallest item has highest priority
tasks = []
heapq.heappush(tasks, (3, "low priority task"))
heapq.heappush(tasks, (1, "urgent task"))
heapq.heappush(tasks, (2, "medium task"))

# Always extracts the smallest (highest priority) element
print(heapq.heappop(tasks))  # (1, 'urgent task')
print(heapq.heappop(tasks))  # (2, 'medium task')

# Max-heap: negate the priority
heapq.heappush(tasks, (-5, "most urgent"))
print(heapq.heappop(tasks))  # (-5, 'most urgent') → priority 5

items.text: — O(n) to convert an unsorted list into a heap in-place

runs.text: Priority queues power Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm, A* search, Huffman coding, top-K queries, and event-driven simulation.
operates on a regular list — it imposes heap structure on the list but does not create a separate object. The heap invariant is maintained only if you always use

A priority queue is an emergency room triage system: patients do not get seen in the order they arrived — the most critical patient is always seen next, regardless of when they showed up. The heap is the triage nurse who constantly re-sorts the waiting room.

cards.title: Circular Buffer (Ring Buffer)
cards.teaser: A circular buffer is a fixed-size queue implemented as an array that wraps around — when the write pointer reaches the end of the array, it loops back to index 0. It delivers O(1) enqueue and dequeue with zero memory allocation after initialization.

runs.text: A circular buffer (also called a ring buffer) uses a fixed-size array with two pointers —
(rear, write pointer). Both pointers advance with each operation using modular arithmetic (
), wrapping around when they reach the end of the array.

items.text: Zero heap allocation after initialization — critical for real-time systems and embedded software
CPU cache-friendly — the array is contiguous in memory unlike a linked list
Used in OS kernel I/O buffers, audio streaming, network packet buffers, and log rotation
is a bounded deque that evicts the oldest item on overflow — it approximates circular buffer behavior for most application-level use cases

runs.text: A circular buffer is like a conveyor belt sushi restaurant with a fixed number of seats. New plates are placed at one end of the belt and removed at the other. When the belt completes a loop, the placement point wraps around to the beginning. The restaurant never grows — it just rotates.

cards.title: Classic Applications: Parentheses Matching, BFS, Undo/Redo
cards.teaser: Three patterns account for most stack and queue usage in real code — parentheses matching uses a stack to verify balanced delimiters, BFS uses a queue to process nodes level-by-level, and undo/redo uses two stacks to move actions forward and backward in time.

runs.text: Recognizing which data structure fits a problem is the skill. These three patterns cover a large fraction of the cases you will encounter.

The pattern selector: if you need to process things in the order they were received, use a queue. If you need to process things in reverse order or trace a path back, use a stack. If order is determined by priority rather than arrival, use a priority queue.

Parentheses matching is like checking if every open door has a corresponding close door in the right order — you note each open door on a notepad (push) and cross it off when you reach the matching close door (pop). BFS is like expanding a rumor by telling all your friends at once before any of them tell their friends. Undo/redo is like a time machine with two tracks: the stack of things you did and the stack of things you undid.

cards.title: queue.Queue for Thread-Safe Queueing
cards.teaser: Python's queue.Queue is the thread-safe queue for producer-consumer workloads — it wraps collections.deque with a mutex and condition variables, blocking producers when the queue is full and blocking consumers when it is empty.

runs.text: When multiple threads share a queue,
is not safe for compound operations (check-then-act). The
module in the standard library provides thread-safe alternatives with built-in blocking:

items.text: — thread-safe priority queue backed by heapq

explanation.code:
import queue
import threading

q = queue.Queue(maxsize=10)  # blocks producers when full

def producer():
    for i in range(20):
        q.put(i)            # blocks if queue is full
    q.put(None)             # sentinel to signal done

def consumer():
    while True:
        item = q.get()      # blocks if queue is empty
        if item is None:
            break
        print(f"processed {item}")
        q.task_done()       # signals that this item is done

producer_thread = threading.Thread(target=producer)
consumer_thread = threading.Thread(target=consumer)
producer_thread.start()
consumer_thread.start()
producer_thread.join()
consumer_thread.join()

— dequeue; blocks by default if empty

queue.Queue is like a warehouse loading dock with a supervisor. Trucks (producers) can only drop off packages when there is a free bay — if the dock is full, they wait in the parking lot. Forklifts (consumers) pick up packages when they arrive — if the dock is empty, they idle. The supervisor (mutex and condition variables) ensures no truck and forklift ever crash into each other.
